Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them leaders (a'immah) and to make them the inheritors﴾ ﴿and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they were wary of﴾ ﴿And We inspired the mother of Moses: "Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river (al-yamm), and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers."﴾

The meaning: Pharaoh oppressed them, and We wish to bestow blessing and to magnify the favour upon those who were oppressed. And "al-a'immah" are those in charge of affairs. Qatadah said: ﴿and make them the inheritors﴾ means the land of Egypt and al-Sham. Al-A'mash recited "wa-li-numakkina" with a lam. The majority recited "wa-nurya Fir'awna" with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the ra', a fatha on the ya', and a nasb on "Fir'awna". Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa-yara" with a ya', a fatha on the ra', and a sukun on the ya', as a past-tense verb with the subject being Pharaoh and those after him. The meaning is: Pharaoh, his people and his hosts fall into what they feared and were wary of from the direction of the Children of Israel and their ascendancy. Haman is the vizier of Pharaoh and the greatest of his men; he is mentioned because of his standing in disbelief and his prominence among his people, so in this context he has humiliation and a curse, not honour.

As for this "inspiration" (wahy) to the mother of Moses, a group said it was a saying in her dream; Qatadah said it was an inspiration (ilham); and a group said it was through an angel who appeared to her. All agreed that she was not a prophetess, and the sending of the angel to her was like the speaking of angels to people without prophethood, as in the well-known hadith about the leper, the bald man, and other reports of angels speaking to people without prophethood.

The sum of the matter of the mother of Moses is that she knew that what came into her heart was from Allah and a promise from Him. This is required by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We returned him to his mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve and would know that the promise of Allah is true﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that she might be among the believers﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], i.e., by the promise. As-Suddi and others said: she was commanded to suckle him immediately after birth and to do with him what is in the verse, because the fear occurred right after birth. Ibn Jurayj said: she was commanded to suckle him for four months in a garden, and when she feared that he would cry because her milk did not suffice him, she did this with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more apparent, except that the latter is supported by two matters. One of them is His saying: ﴿when you fear for him﴾, and "idha" is a time-adverb for what is future; the other is that he did not accept the wet-nurses, and an infant immediately after birth does not do that, unless this was from him because Allah, blessed and exalted, forbade the breasts to him and made him refuse them, unlike other infants. Amr ibn 'Abd al-Wahid recited "an arda'ihi" with a kasra on the nun, as an irregular (i'tibat) form, not a lightening, while the common light form is with a fatha on the nun; this was said by Ibn Jinni. Al-Mahdawi attributed this recitation to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him. "Al-yamm" means the bulk and main body of water, and what is intended is the Nile of Egypt.

It is related in the narratives of this verse that the mother of Moses, peace be upon him (her name being Yuhanah), took him and wrapped him in his clothes, made for him a small chest, locked it upon him, hung its key on him, and entrusted him, out of trust in Allah and waiting for His promise. When he went out of her sight, her fear returned to her and she was preoccupied about him; Satan despaired her, so she became anxious about him and nearly exposed the matter, and his sister began to follow him, i.e., to trace his trail.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them leaders (a'immah) and to make them the inheritors﴾ ﴿and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they were wary of﴾ ﴿And We inspired the mother of Moses: "Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river (al-yamm), and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers."﴾

The meaning: Pharaoh oppressed them, and We wish to bestow blessing and to magnify the favour upon those who were oppressed. And "al-a'immah" are those in charge of affairs. Qatadah said: ﴿and make them the inheritors﴾ means the land of Egypt and al-Sham. Al-A'mash recited "wa-li-numakkina" with a lam. The majority recited "wa-nurya Fir'awna" with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the ra', a fatha on the ya', and a nasb on "Fir'awna". Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa-yara" with a ya', a fatha on the ra', and a sukun on the ya', as a past-tense verb with the subject being Pharaoh and those after him. The meaning is: Pharaoh, his people and his hosts fall into what they feared and were wary of from the direction of the Children of Israel and their ascendancy. Haman is the vizier of Pharaoh and the greatest of his men; he is mentioned because of his standing in disbelief and his prominence among his people, so in this context he has humiliation and a curse, not honour.

As for this "inspiration" (wahy) to the mother of Moses, a group said it was a saying in her dream; Qatadah said it was an inspiration (ilham); and a group said it was through an angel who appeared to her. All agreed that she was not a prophetess, and the sending of the angel to her was like the speaking of angels to people without prophethood, as in the well-known hadith about the leper, the bald man, and other reports of angels speaking to people without prophethood.

The sum of the matter of the mother of Moses is that she knew that what came into her heart was from Allah and a promise from Him. This is required by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We returned him to his mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve and would know that the promise of Allah is true﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that she might be among the believers﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], i.e., by the promise. As-Suddi and others said: she was commanded to suckle him immediately after birth and to do with him what is in the verse, because the fear occurred right after birth. Ibn Jurayj said: she was commanded to suckle him for four months in a garden, and when she feared that he would cry because her milk did not suffice him, she did this with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more apparent, except that the latter is supported by two matters. One of them is His saying: ﴿when you fear for him﴾, and "idha" is a time-adverb for what is future; the other is that he did not accept the wet-nurses, and an infant immediately after birth does not do that, unless this was from him because Allah, blessed and exalted, forbade the breasts to him and made him refuse them, unlike other infants. The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 28, verses 8–11:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were ever sinners.﴾ ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said, "A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son," while they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void. She was about to reveal it, had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers.﴾ ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from afar while they did not notice.﴾

Al-iltiqat (التقاط, picking up) means meeting without intention. From it is the saying of the poet:

"A watering place I came upon by chance,
I did not meet, when I came to it, any who had gone before."

*Al-Ali Fir'awn* (آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ, the family of Pharaoh) means his people. It is narrated that Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, saw the chest floating on the river, so she ordered that it be brought to her and opened. In it she saw a small child, and she had mercy on him and loved him. Al-Suddi said: her maidservants had a basin in the palace on the Nile, into which the water flowed to the palace, so that they could use it for their needs and benefits. While they were washing in that basin, the chest came, and they carried it to their mistress. Ibn Ishaq said: Pharaoh saw it floating and ordered it brought, and Asiya was sitting with him, and so what has been mentioned occurred.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that he might become for them an enemy﴾ is the *lam al-'aqiba* (لامُ العاقِبَةِ, the lam of consequence), not that the purpose of the picking up was for him to become an enemy. The majority read *wa-hazanan* (وَحَزَنا) with a fatha on the ha. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talha and al-A'mash read *wa-huznan* (وَحُزْنًا) with a damma on the ha and sukun on the zay. *Al-Khati'* (الخاطِئُ) is one who deliberately commits error, while *al-mukhti'* (المُخْطِئُ) is one who does not intend it.

The commentators differed about the time at which Pharaoh's wife said: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾. One group said: it was at the time of picking up the chest, when she informed Pharaoh of it, because it occurred to him that he was from the Children of Israel, and that this was done in order to escape the slaughter. So he said, "Bring me the slaughterers." His wife said what has been mentioned, and Pharaoh said, "As for me, no." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If he had said yes, he would have believed in Moses, and he would have been a comfort of the eye for him." Al-Suddi said: rather, she raised him until he grew up. Pharaoh saw in him nobility and thought he was from the Children of Israel, and took him in his hand. Moses, peace be upon him, stretched out his hand and plucked the beard of Pharaoh. Then Pharaoh resolved to slaughter him. At that time she spoke to him with this, and tested him with a live coal and a ruby, and his tongue was burned. His saying ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ means they did not perceive that he would be the one through whose hands the kingdom would be destroyed. This was said by Qatada and others. Ibn Mas'ud read: "Do not kill him; a comfort of the eye for me and for you," placing the words before and after.

His saying "*wa-asbaha*" (وَأصْبَحَ, and became) is an expression for the continuation and settling of a state, and it is like *zalla* (ظَلَّ, remained). From it is the saying of Abu Sufyan to al-Abbas on the day of the Conquest: "Indeed the kingdom of your nephew has become great today," meaning: his state settled as great.

Most people read *fari'an* (فارِغًا, void) from *al-faragh* (الفراغ, emptiness). Its meaning has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: void of everything except the remembrance of Moses, peace be upon him. Malik said: it is the going away of reason.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their hearts void﴾ [Ibrahim: 43]. Another group said: void of patience. Ibn Zayd said: void of the promise of Allah, blessed and exalted, and His revelation to her; that is, she forgot it because of worry, and its trace weakened in her soul. Iblis said to her: "You fled with him from a killing in which there would have been reward for you, and you killed him with your own hand." Abu 'Ubayda said: void of grief, since he had not drowned. Fadala ibn 'Ubayd (it is said: Ibn 'Ubayda) and al-Hasan read *fazaʿan* (فَزَعًا, fear) from *al-faza'* (الفزع), with fa and zay. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read *qar'an* (قَرْعًا) with qaf and ra, from *al-qari'a* (القارِعَةُ), which is a great worry. Some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, read *faraghan* (فَرَغا) with a kasra on the fa, a sakin ra, and a dotted ghayn. Its meaning is: going away in vain, destroyed from worry and grief. From it is the saying of Talīha al-Asadi:

"If their souls were struck in killing,
they shall not go away in vain by the killing of the Hibal."

That is: in vain, destroyed, of no benefit. Khalil ibn Ahmad read *furughan* (فُرُغًا) with a damma on the fa and ra.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed she was about to reveal it﴾ means the matter of her son. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mother of Moses was about to say: 'Woe to my son!' and would have come out crying, with her face bare." *Al-Rabt 'ala al-qalb* (الرَّبْطُ عَلى القَلْبِ, binding upon the heart) means comforting and strengthening it. From it is the saying about the brave and the patient in tight situations: *rabit al-ja'sh* (رابِطُ الجَأْشِ, steady of heart). Qatada said: and He bound upon her heart with faith. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that she would be among the believers﴾ means among those who affirm the promise of Allah, blessed and exalted, and what He revealed to her.

Then she said to the sister of Moses, out of hope and seeking for him: "Follow him." *Al-qass* (القَصُّ) is the seeking of a trace. It is narrated that his sister went out into the streets of the city, searching in disguise. She saw him with people from the entourage of the family of Pharaoh, who were seeking for him a woman to nurse him, since he had refused the nurses. *"'An junub"* (﴿عن جُنُبٍ﴾) means from a side, without intention and without closeness that would make them aware of her. It is said: *'an janaba* (عن جَنابَةٍ) and *'an janab* (عن جَنابٍ). From it is the saying of the poet:

"A dove reminded me from afar, at 'Usfan, of my family, while the heart was grieved."

From *al-janaba* is the saying of al-A'sha:

"I came to Hurayth visiting from afar, while Hurayth was stiff toward my gift."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of these expressions is: from a place at a side, or from a distance. The meaning of the verse is: from a distance, you did not come near him so that he would notice her. Abu 'Ubayda recited for 'Alqama:

"So do not deprive me of a gift from afar, for I am a man strange in the midst of the tents."

Qatada read *'an janbin* (عن جَنْبٍ) with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the nun. This is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'raj. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim read *'an janibin* (عن جانِبٍ). The majority read *'an junubin* (عن جُنُبٍ) with a damma on the jim and the nun.

This is among the subtle kindnesses of Allah, blessed and exalted, to him and to his mother, according to the promise that was revealed to her. Qatada said: the meaning of *'an junubin* is that she looked at him as if she wanted him.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read *qar'an* (قَرْعًا) with qaf and ra, from *al-qari'a* (القارِعَةُ), which is a great worry. Some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, read *faraghan* (فَرَغا) with a kasra on the fa, a sakin ra, and a dotted ghayn. Its meaning is: going away in vain, destroyed from worry and grief. From it is the saying of Talīha al-Asadi:

"If their souls were struck in killing,
they shall not go away in vain by the killing of the Hibal."

That is: in vain, destroyed, of no benefit. Khalil ibn Ahmad read *furughan* (فُرُغًا) with a damma on the fa and ra.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed she was about to reveal it﴾ means the matter of her son. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mother of Moses was about to say: 'Woe to my son!' and would have come out crying, with her face bare." *Al-Rabt 'ala al-qalb* (الرَّبْطُ عَلى القَلْبِ, binding upon the heart) means comforting and strengthening it. From it is the saying about the brave and the patient in tight situations: *rabit al-ja'sh* (رابِطُ الجَأْشِ, steady of heart). Qatada said: and He bound upon her heart with faith. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that she would be among the believers﴾ means among those who affirm the promise of Allah, blessed and exalted, and what He revealed to her.

Then she said to the sister of Moses, out of hope and seeking for him: "Follow him." *Al-qass* (القَصُّ) is the seeking of a trace. It is narrated that his sister went out into the streets of the city, searching in disguise. She saw him with people from the entourage of the family of Pharaoh, who were seeking for him a woman to nurse him, since he had refused the nurses. *"'An junub"* (﴿عن جُنُبٍ﴾) means from a side, without intention and without closeness that would make them aware of her. It is said: *'an janaba* (عن جَنابَةٍ) and *'an janab* (عن جَنابٍ). From it is the saying of the poet:

"A dove reminded me from afar, at 'Usfan, of my family, while the heart was grieved."

From *al-janaba* is the saying of al-A'sha:

"I came to Hurayth visiting from afar, while Hurayth was stiff toward my gift."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of these expressions is: from a place at a side, or from a distance. The meaning of the verse is: from a distance, you did not come near him so that he would notice her. Abu 'Ubayda recited for 'Alqama:

"So do not deprive me of a gift from afar, for I am a man strange in the midst of the tents."

Qatada read *'an janbin* (عن جَنْبٍ) with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the nun. This is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'raj. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim read *'an janibin* (عن جانِبٍ). The majority read *'an junubin* (عن جُنُبٍ) with a damma on the jim and the nun.

This is a dialect of Judham, who say *janabtu ila liqa'ika* (جَنَبْتُ إلى لِقائِكَ), meaning: I longed for your meeting. Qatada said: the meaning of *'an junubin* is that she looked at him as if she wanted him.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 28, verses 8–11:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were ever sinners.﴾ ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said, "A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son," while they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void. She was about to reveal it, had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers.﴾ ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from afar while they did not notice.﴾

Al-iltiqat (التقاط, picking up) means meeting without intention. From it is the saying of the poet:

"A watering place I came upon by chance,
I did not meet, when I came to it, any who had gone before."

*Al-Ali Fir'awn* (آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ, the family of Pharaoh) means his people. It is narrated that Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, saw the chest floating on the river, so she ordered that it be brought to her and opened. In it she saw a small child, and she had mercy on him and loved him. Al-Suddi said: her maidservants had a basin in the palace on the Nile, into which the water flowed to the palace, so that they could use it for their needs and benefits. While they were washing in that basin, the chest came, and they carried it to their mistress. Ibn Ishaq said: Pharaoh saw it floating and ordered it brought, and Asiya was sitting with him, and so what has been mentioned occurred.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that he might become for them an enemy﴾ is the *lam al-'aqiba* (لامُ العاقِبَةِ, the lam of consequence), not that the purpose of the picking up was for him to become an enemy. The majority read *wa-hazanan* (وَحَزَنا) with a fatha on the ha. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talha and al-A'mash read *wa-huznan* (وَحُزْنًا) with a damma on the ha and sukun on the zay. *Al-Khati'* (الخاطِئُ) is one who deliberately commits error, while *al-mukhti'* (المُخْطِئُ) is one who does not intend it.

The commentators differed about the time at which Pharaoh's wife said: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾. One group said: it was at the time of picking up the chest, when she informed Pharaoh of it, because it occurred to him that he was from the Children of Israel, and that this was done in order to escape the slaughter. So he said, "Bring me the slaughterers." His wife said what has been mentioned, and Pharaoh said, "As for me, no." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If he had said yes, he would have believed in Moses, and he would have been a comfort of the eye for him." Al-Suddi said: rather, she raised him until he grew up. Pharaoh saw in him nobility and thought he was from the Children of Israel, and took him in his hand. Moses, peace be upon him, stretched out his hand and plucked the beard of Pharaoh. Then Pharaoh resolved to slaughter him. At that time she spoke to him with this, and tested him with a live coal and a ruby, and his tongue was burned. His saying ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ means they did not perceive that he would be the one through whose hands the kingdom would be destroyed. This was said by Qatada and others. Ibn Mas'ud read: "Do not kill him; a comfort of the eye for me and for you," placing the words before and after.

His saying "*wa-asbaha*" (وَأصْبَحَ, and became) is an expression for the continuation and settling of a state, and it is like *zalla* (ظَلَّ, remained). From it is the saying of Abu Sufyan to al-Abbas on the day of the Conquest: "Indeed the kingdom of your nephew has become great today," meaning: his state settled as great.

Most people read *fari'an* (فارِغًا, void) from *al-faragh* (الفراغ, emptiness). Its meaning has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: void of everything except the remembrance of Moses, peace be upon him. Malik said: it is the going away of reason.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Zayd said: void of the promise of Allah, blessed and exalted, and His revelation to her; that is, she forgot it because of worry, and its trace weakened in her soul. Qatada said: the meaning of *'an junubin* is that she looked at him as if she wanted him.

﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses beforehand. So she said, "Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you, and who will be sincere toward him?"﴾ ﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of God is true; but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿And when he reached his full strength (ashudd) and became mature, We gave him judgment (hukm) and knowledge; and thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people, and he found in it two men fighting, one from his own party and the other from his enemy. So the one from his party called on him for help against the one from his enemy, and Musa struck him and put an end to him. He said, "This is from the work of Satan; indeed he is a misguiding, manifest enemy."﴾

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ indicates that God Most High singled him out, in refusing the breasts of women, with something that departs from the custom of infants, and this is a prohibition of aversion (tahrim tabghid). "Al-marāḍi‘" is the plural of "murḍi‘" (wet-nurse), and it is used without the feminine ending (ha' al-ta'nith) because it is not confused with men. His saying, "min qabl" (beforehand), means from the beginning of his affair, and "qabl" is indeclinable (mabni). The pronoun in "faqalat" (she said) refers to the sister of Musa. Al-Naqqash said: her name was Maryam. "Yakfulūnahu" means they will raise him well and nurse him. The people knew that their interlocutor was from the Children of Israel, and it was the custom of the Children of Israel that they would serve as wet-nurses and servants. His saying, ﴿and they are sincere toward him﴾, may be understood as the pronoun returning to the child. So they said to her: "You have recognised him, so tell us who he is?" She said: "I only meant that they are sincere toward the king," and she escaped from them by this interpretation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the pronoun returns to the child, but that the sincerity toward him is because of the kingship and an eagerness to gain favour with him and to be near him. In this passage there is an omission (hadhf) required by the apparent sense, namely that they brought her to the mother of Musa and spoke with her about it, so she suckled him and he accepted her, and she was favoured by this, and he was kind to her and to the people of her household, and her eye was cooled, that is, she was gladdened by that. It is narrated that Pharaoh, may God curse him, said to her: "What is the cause of this child's acceptance of you?" She said to him: "I am sweet-scented, and my milk is good, and the tear of joy is cool, while the eye of the grieving is hot and burning." From this meaning it is said: "qarrat al-‘ayn" (the eye was cooled) and "sakhunat" (became warm). Ya‘qub read "nuqirru" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the qaf. The "promise of God" Most High that is referred to is that which He revealed to her at first, either through an angel or by his appearing in the form of one, or through inspiration (ilham), according to the differing of the exegetes on this matter; and the view of inspiration is weak to describe as "promise." His saying, Most High, ﴿but most of them﴾, means the Copts. "Al-ashudd" is the plural of "shidda" (strength), referring to years. A group said it is the attainment of puberty, which is a period of fifteen years; another group said eighteen years; al-Suddi said twenty; another group said twenty-five; another group said thirty; Mujahid and Ibn ‘Abbas said thirty-three; a great group said thirty-six; Mujahid and Qatada said that "istiwa'" (maturity) is forty years; Makki said: "It is said it is sixty years," and this is weak. "Al-ashudd" is the strength of the body, the firmness of its frame and its vigour. "Istawa" means that his intellect and sound judgment were perfected, and this, according to the majority, is at forty. "Al-hukm" is wisdom (hikma), and "al-‘ilm" is knowledge of the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and it is a preliminary to his prophethood, peace be upon him.

The commentators differed concerning the Exalted's saying, ﴿and he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾. Al-Suddi said: At the time of this story Musa was in the habit of attachment to Pharaoh, and he would ride in his processions, to the extent that he was called Musa son of Pharaoh. They said: Pharaoh rode one day and set out to a city among the cities of Egypt called Manf. Then Musa, peace be upon him, learned of Pharaoh's riding, so he rode after him and reached that city at the time of midday rest, which is the time of heedlessness; this was related by Ibn ‘Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. He also said: it is what is between the evening and the night prayer (‘atama). Ibn Ishaq said: rather, the city is Egypt itself, and at this time Musa had already shown struggle against Pharaoh and his people in ways they disliked, so he was hiding himself and feared by them. So he entered disguised, wary, and unnoticed by the people. Ibn Zayd said: rather, Pharaoh had cast him off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years, so he was forgotten, and his matter spread, and he came while the people were in heedlessness through their forgetting of his affair and the distance of their time with him. It was also said: it was a day of festival.

The Exalted's saying, ﴿yaqtatilan﴾ (fighting), is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: fighting one another. "Shi‘atuhu" (his party) are the Children of Israel, and "‘aduwwuhu" (his enemy) are the Copts. Al-Akhfash Sa‘id ibn Mas‘ada mentioned that some read "fa-isti‘anahu" with an unpointed ‘ayn, but that is a copyist's error (tashif), not a recitation. Al-Tha‘labi mentioned that the one "from his party" was al-Samiri, and that the other was Pharaoh's cook.

The Exalted's saying, ﴿This﴾, and "wa-hadha" (and this), is a narration of a state that had been present, and for this reason "this" is used for an absent past event. Al-Tha‘labi related that in the codex of Ibn Mas‘ud it is "fa-nakazahu," and the meaning is the same. "Qada ‘alayhi" means he killed him. Musa, peace and blessings be upon him, had not intended to kill the Coptic man, but his blow coincided with the appointed term, and his death came from it. So Musa, peace be upon him, regretted it, and considered that it was an incitement of Satan into his hand, and that the anger which accompanied that blow was from Satan and from his prompting; and he himself stated this, and in this respect he made it "from his work." The excess of his strength, peace be upon him, was by exceeding what he intended at the time of his anger, by more than he intended.

So the one from his party called on him for help against the one from his enemy, and Musa struck him and put an end to him. He said, "This is from the work of Satan; indeed he is a misguiding, manifest enemy."﴾

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ indicates that God Most High singled him out, in refusing the breasts of women, with something that departs from the custom of infants, and this is a prohibition of aversion (tahrim tabghid). "Al-marāḍi‘" is the plural of "murḍi‘" (wet-nurse), and it is used without the feminine ending (ha' al-ta'nith) because it is not confused with men. His saying, "min qabl" (beforehand), means from the beginning of his affair, and "qabl" is indeclinable (mabni). The pronoun in "faqalat" (she said) refers to the sister of Musa. Al-Naqqash said: her name was Maryam. "Yakfulūnahu" means they will raise him well and nurse him. The people knew that their interlocutor was from the Children of Israel, and it was the custom of the Children of Israel that they would serve as wet-nurses and servants. His saying, ﴿and they are sincere toward him﴾, may be understood as the pronoun returning to the child. So they said to her: "You have recognised him, so tell us who he is?" She said: "I only meant that they are sincere toward the king," and she escaped from them by this interpretation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the pronoun returns to the child, but that the sincerity toward him is because of the kingship and an eagerness to gain favour with him and to be near him. In this passage there is an omission (hadhf) required by the apparent sense, namely that they brought her to the mother of Musa and spoke with her about it, so she suckled him and he accepted her, and she was favoured by this, and he was kind to her and to the people of her household, and her eye was cooled, that is, she was gladdened by that. It is narrated that Pharaoh, may God curse him, said to her: "What is the cause of this child's acceptance of you?" She said to him: "I am sweet-scented, and my milk is good, and the tear of joy is cool, while the eye of the grieving is hot and burning." From this meaning it is said: "qarrat al-‘ayn" (the eye was cooled) and "sakhunat" (became warm). Ya‘qub read "nuqirru" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the qaf. The "promise of God" Most High that is referred to is that which He revealed to her at first, either through an angel or by his appearing in the form of one, or through inspiration (ilham), according to the differing of the exegetes on this matter; and the view of inspiration is weak to describe as "promise." His saying, Most High, ﴿but most of them﴾, means the Copts. "Al-ashudd" is the plural of "shidda" (strength), referring to years. A group said it is the attainment of puberty, which is a period of fifteen years; another group said eighteen years; al-Suddi said twenty; another group said twenty-five; another group said thirty; Mujahid and Ibn ‘Abbas said thirty-three; a great group said thirty-six; Mujahid and Qatada said that "istiwa'" (maturity) is forty years; Makki said: "It is said it is sixty years," and this is weak. "Al-ashudd" is the strength of the body, the firmness of its frame and its vigour. "Istawa" means that his intellect and sound judgment were perfected, and this, according to the majority, is at forty. "Al-hukm" is wisdom (hikma), and "al-‘ilm" is knowledge of the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and it is a preliminary to his prophethood, peace be upon him.

The commentators differed concerning the Exalted's saying, ﴿and he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾. Al-Suddi said: At the time of this story Musa was in the habit of attachment to Pharaoh, and he would ride in his processions, to the extent that he was called Musa son of Pharaoh. They said: Pharaoh rode one day and set out to a city among the cities of Egypt called Manf. Then Musa, peace be upon him, learned of Pharaoh's riding, so he rode after him and reached that city at the time of midday rest, which is the time of heedlessness; this was related by Ibn ‘Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. He also said: it is what is between the evening and the night prayer (‘atama). Ibn Ishaq said: rather, the city is Egypt itself, and at this time Musa had already shown struggle against Pharaoh and his people in ways they disliked, so he was hiding himself and feared by them. So he entered disguised, wary, and unnoticed by the people. Ibn Zayd said: rather, Pharaoh had cast him off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years, so he was forgotten, and his matter spread, and he came while the people were in heedlessness through their forgetting of his affair and the distance of their time with him. It was also said: it was a day of festival.

The Exalted's saying, ﴿yaqtatilan﴾ (fighting), is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: fighting one another. "Shi‘atuhu" (his party) are the Children of Israel, and "‘aduwwuhu" (his enemy) are the Copts. Al-Akhfash Sa‘id ibn Mas‘ada mentioned that some read "fa-isti‘anahu" with an unpointed ‘ayn, but that is a copyist's error (tashif), not a recitation. Al-Tha‘labi mentioned that the one "from his party" was al-Samiri, and that the other was Pharaoh's cook.

The Exalted's saying, ﴿This﴾, and "wa-hadha" (and this), is a narration of a state that had been present, and for this reason "this" is used for an absent past event. "Al-wakz" is striking with the hand gathered into a fist like the knot of the three and seventy; Ibn Mas‘ud read "fa-lakazahu," and the meaning is the same, except that "al-lakz" is on the jaw; "al-wakz" is by metathesis (qalb). Al-Tha‘labi related that in the codex of Ibn Mas‘ud it is "fa-nakazahu," and the meaning is the same. "Qada ‘alayhi" means he killed him. Musa, peace and blessings be upon him, had not intended to kill the Coptic man, but his blow coincided with the appointed term, and his death came from it. So Musa, peace be upon him, regretted it, and considered that it was an incitement of Satan into his hand, and that the anger which accompanied that blow was from Satan and from his prompting; and he himself stated this, and in this respect he made it "from his work." The excess of his strength, peace be upon him, was by exceeding what he intended at the time of his anger, by more than he intended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 16–18:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." So He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾ ﴿So he became fearful in the city, anticipating [news], when suddenly the one who had sought his help the previous day was calling out to him for help. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a person of error."﴾

Then, indeed, the remorse of Moses, peace be upon him, moved him to humble himself before his Lord, the Exalted, and to seek forgiveness for his sin. So He forgave him that error. Qatadah said: "By Allah, he recognised the way out, so he sought forgiveness."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He, peace be upon him, continued to repeat this about himself, although he knew that He had forgiven him, to the extent that on the Day of Resurrection he says: "And I killed a soul for which I had not been commanded to kill," as is authentically related in the hadith of the intercession.

Then he, peace be upon him, said, making a covenant with his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic: "My Lord, by Your blessing upon me and because of Your kindness and Your forgiveness, I am committed not to be a helper of the criminals." This is the best of what has been interpreted [of this verse]. Al-Tabari said: "It is an oath; he swore by the blessing of Allah, Blessed and Exalted." This is weakened by the form of the answer to the oath, for it is not properly suited to His saying: ﴿fa-lan akuna﴾ ("so I will never be"), because an oath is not introduced by "lan," and the fa' prevents "lan" from being treated as "la" or "ma." So reflect on this. Al-Tabari also argued from the reading of 'Abdullah: "fa-la taj'alni zahiran" ("so do not make me a supporter").

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The people of virtue and knowledge have used this verse to prohibit serving the unjust and assisting them in any of their affairs, and they held that the verse encompasses this. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah explicitly stated this.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿fa-asbaha fi'l-madinati khaifan﴾ ("so he became fearful in the city") is an expression meaning that he was in a state of constant fear at all times, just as you say: "Zayd became knowledgeable" (asbaha Zaydun 'aliman). And "yataraqqabu" (anticipating) means: there is a watcher over him for his act of killing, so he is on the lookout (yatahassasu). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He passed while in a state of watchfulness, and suddenly that Israelite who had fought the Copt the previous day was fighting another man from the Copts. The killing of the Copt had been concealed from the people and kept secret. When the Israelite saw him, he called out to him for help (istaṣrakhahu), meaning he cried out to him seeking aid. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Whenever a fearful crier came to us, the shouting was for him like the striking of the water-skins."

When Moses, peace be upon him, saw him fighting that other man, he was greatly displeased by it, and said to him, rebuking and reproaching him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a person of error.﴾ Moses nonetheless intended to help the Israelite. When he approached them both, the Israelite felt his presence and was frightened of him, thinking that he might strike him, and he was frightened by the strength he had seen the previous day, and he had witnessed the matter of the slain man.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 19–21:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So when he (Moses) wished to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, he said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You intend only to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not intend to be among the reformers."﴾ ﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, hastening. He said: "O Moses, the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you, so leave; indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers."﴾ ﴿So he left from there, fearful and watchful. He said: "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people."﴾

The majority of people recited "yabtishu" (يَبْطِشُ) with a kasra on the ta' (ṭāʾ), while al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far recited it with a damma on the ta'. Both are dialectal forms (lughatān). The Israelite said to Moses, in effect, through his tongue, and fled from him, so the matter of the slain man became known. Tyrants (al-jabābira) are characterized by killing people without right; therefore the Israelite treated Moses as such and denied him reform (al-iṣlāḥ). Al-Sha'bi said: whoever kills two men is a tyrant. Al-Sha'bi also said: when it became widely known that Moses had killed the slain man, and the statement of the Israelite tended to dominate people's minds, so that they believed it against Moses, together with what Moses, peace be upon him, already had of antecedents, namely that he was the one indicated as the cause of the corruption of the kingdom, Pharaoh sent to him men from his soldiers to seek him and bring him for execution. So he went out on the main road, and a man—it is said he was a believer from the family of Pharaoh, and it is said he was someone else—took a route through the side paths of the road, intending the place of Moses, reached him, and said to him: "Indeed the chiefs" (the verse).

"Yasʿā" (يَسْعى) means: he walks quickly, hastening in his walking, as said by al-Zajjaj and others; it is less than running. Ibn al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "he hurries," and it is not running at full speed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the sa'y to the Friday prayer, and the first (interpretation) is, in my opinion, more apparent in this verse.

"Ya'tamirun" (يَأْتَمِرُونَ) is of the pattern yaftaʿilūna, and the yaftaʿilu form frequently comes with the meaning of yatafāʿalu, from which comes izdawaja meaning tazawwaja. Ibn Qutayba held that it means "some of them command others," and said: had that been the case, it would have been "yatā'amarūn."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He overlooked that yaftaʿila can mean yatafāʿala. In the Qur'an: ﴿And consult among yourselves in good manner﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

؎ I see people have introduced a custom, and in every new event it is deliberated upon.

Al-Tabari recited:

؎ Whatever you deliberate among us, your command is in your right hand or your left.

And from it is the saying of Rabi'a ibn Jathm:

؎ O Ibn Ka'b, as if I were a stray, and what is deliberated against a man is spread upon him.

Moses, peace be upon him, went out and escaped from the people, and they did not find him. By the urgency of his fear he went out onto the road to Madyan, which is the city of the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. Moses, peace be upon him, did not know that road and had not accompanied anyone, so he took its unknown way, trusting in Allah, the Exalted, and relying upon Him. قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿وَلَمّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلْقاءَ مَدْيَنَ قالَ عَسى رَبِّي أنْ يَهْدِيَنِي سَواءَ السَبِيلِ﴾ ﴿وَلَمّا ورَدَ ماءَ مَدْيَنَ وجَدَ عَلَيْهِ أُمَّةً مِنَ الناسِ يَسْقُونَ ووَجَدَ مِنَ دُونِهِمُ امْرَأتَيْنِ تَذُودانِ قالَ ما خَطْبُكُما قالَتا لا نَسْقِي (p-٥٨٣)حَتّى يُصْدِرَ الرِعاءُ وأبُونا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾ ﴿فَسَقى لَهُما ثُمَّ تَوَلّى إلى الظِلِّ فَقالَ رَبِّ إنِّي لِما أنْزَلْتَ إلَيَّ مِن خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ﴾

When he (peace be upon him) left, fleeing by himself, alone, barefoot, with nothing with him, he saw his condition, his lack of knowledge of the road, and his having no provisions or anything else. So he entrusted his affair to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and said: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way﴾. These statements from him indicate that he was one who knew Allah, Exalted is He, and was learned in the wisdom and knowledge that Allah had given him. "Tawajjaha" means he turned his face toward it. "Tilqaa'" means toward a direction, i.e., toward the side in which the thing mentioned is encountered. ﴿Sawa' al-sabil﴾ means its middle. At this time Allah sent the angel who guided him, as we mentioned earlier. Mujahid said: by ﴿sawa' al-sabil﴾ he meant the road to Madyan. Al-Hasan said: he meant the path of guidance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is more eloquent. Its parallel is the saying of al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), reporting from the Prophet (ﷺ): "This is the one who guides the way," the hadith. So he (peace be upon him) walked until he arrived at Madyan, meaning he reached it. His arrival at the water means his reaching it, because he entered it. The word "wurud" may mean entering into a thing, and it may mean overlooking it and reaching it even if one does not enter it. So Musa's arrival at this water was by reaching it. These senses of the word are included in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71]. "Madyan" is not declined, since it is a well-known town. "Ummah" means a large group. "Yasqun" means their livestock. ﴿Min dunihim﴾ means on a side toward the direction from which he had come, so he reached the two women before reaching the group, and likewise they were ﴿min dunihim﴾ relative to him. "Tadhudan" means they hold back and restrain. From it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Surely men will be driven away from my basin," the hadith. Evidence for this meaning in poetry is abundant. In some of the codices the reading is "two women restraining, tadhudan." There is disagreement about "dhawd." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and others said: they hold back their sheep from the water, fearing the strong watering men. Qatadah said: they hold back the people from their sheep. When Musa (peace be upon him) saw the two women he said: ﴿What is your business?﴾, meaning: what is your affair and situation? It seems that the use of asking with "khatb" is only for someone afflicted, oppressed, one deserving pity, or one who has come with something objectionable, so it is as though he assumed in general that there was some harm. They informed him of their situation, and that their father was a very old man. The meaning is that he, because of his weakness, cannot undertake the matter of their sheep, and that they, because of their weakness and little strength, cannot compete with the strong. Their custom was to wait until the shepherds, i.e. the people, had left the water and it was empty, and then they would come. Another group said: the wells were uncovered, and the crowding of people prevented them. So when Musa wanted to water for them, he pushed the people aside and overpowered them at the water until he had watered. It is because of this overpowering that he did that one of the two described him as strong. Another group said: rather, their wells had large stones over their mouths, and the coming of the two women followed what remained in the troughs of drink, the leftovers that remained for the waterers. Musa (peace be upon him) went to a well that was covered, while the people watered from other than it, and its stone could be lifted only by seven men, as stated by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jurayj said ten. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said thirty. al-Zajjaj said forty. So Musa (peace be upon him) lifted it and watered for the two women. Because of his lifting of the rock, one described him as strong. It was also said: their well was one, and he lifted the stone from it after the waterers had departed, since the custom of the two women was to drink the leftovers.

Al-Jumhur read "nasqi" with a fathah on the nun. Talhah read "nasqi" with a dammah. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "hatta yasdura" with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the dal, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Qatadah. The rest read "yusdira" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the dal, with the object omitted, its implied object being: their livestock. Omission of the object is common in the Qur'an and in speech. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Talhah, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa. "Al-ri'a'" is the plural of "ra'in," a shepherd.

Musa (peace be upon him) turned to the shade of a samurah tree, as said by Ibn Mas'ud. He implicitly sought what he might eat through his saying: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, and he did not explicitly ask. Thus all the exegetes related that in these words he sought what he would eat. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: Hunger had reached him to the extent that his color had turned green from eating herbs, and he became so weak that his belly stuck to his back, and the greenness of the herbs could be seen in his belly, and on that day he was the most honored of creation before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is related that he did not reach Madyan until the soles of his feet had worn away. In this there is a lesson, and a judgment on the worthlessness of this world before Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

"Yasqun" means their livestock. ﴿Min dunihim﴾ means on a side toward the direction from which he had come, so he reached the two women before reaching the group, and likewise they were ﴿min dunihim﴾ relative to him. "Tadhudan" means they hold back and restrain. From it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Surely men will be driven away from my basin," the hadith. Evidence for this meaning in poetry is abundant. In some of the codices the reading is "two women restraining, tadhudan." There is disagreement about "dhawd." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and others said: they hold back their sheep from the water, fearing the strong watering men. Qatadah said: they hold back the people from their sheep. When Musa (peace be upon him) saw the two women he said: ﴿What is your business?﴾, meaning: what is your affair and situation? It seems that the use of asking with "khatb" is only for someone afflicted, oppressed, one deserving pity, or one who has come with something objectionable, so it is as though he assumed in general that there was some harm. They informed him of their situation, and that their father was a very old man. The meaning is that he, because of his weakness, cannot undertake the matter of their sheep, and that they, because of their weakness and little strength, cannot compete with the strong. Their custom was to wait until the shepherds, i.e. the people, had left the water and it was empty, and then they would come. Another group said: the wells were uncovered, and the crowding of people prevented them. So when Musa wanted to water for them, he pushed the people aside and overpowered them at the water until he had watered. It is because of this overpowering that he did that one of the two described him as strong. Another group said: rather, their wells had large stones over their mouths, and the coming of the two women followed what remained in the troughs of drink, the leftovers that remained for the waterers. Musa (peace be upon him) went to a well that was covered, while the people watered from other than it, and its stone could be lifted only by seven men, as stated by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jurayj said ten. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said thirty. al-Zajjaj said forty. So Musa (peace be upon him) lifted it and watered for the two women. Because of his lifting of the rock, one described him as strong. It was also said: their well was one, and he lifted the stone from it after the waterers had departed, since the custom of the two women was to drink the leftovers.

Al-Jumhur read "nasqi" with a fathah on the nun. Talhah read "nasqi" with a dammah. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "hatta yasdura" with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the dal, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Qatadah. The rest read "yusdira" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the dal, with the object omitted, its implied object being: their livestock. Omission of the object is common in the Qur'an and in speech. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Talhah, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa. "Al-ri'a'" is the plural of "ra'in," a shepherd.

Musa (peace be upon him) turned to the shade of a samurah tree, as said by Ibn Mas'ud. He implicitly sought what he might eat through his saying: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, and he did not explicitly ask. Thus all the exegetes related that in these words he sought what he would eat. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: Hunger had reached him to the extent that his color had turned green from eating herbs, and he became so weak that his belly stuck to his back, and the greenness of the herbs could be seen in his belly, and on that day he was the most honored of creation before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is related that he did not reach Madyan until the soles of his feet had worn away. In this there is a lesson, and a judgment on the worthlessness of this world before Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 25–27:

The words of the Most High:

﴿So one of the two women came to him, walking shyly. She said, "Indeed, my father invites you so that he may reward you for what you watered for us." And when he came to him and related to him the story, he said, "Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿One of the two said, "O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on the condition that you serve me for eight years. But if you complete ten, it is from you. And I do not intend to burden you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous."﴾

In this place there is an ellipsis indicated by the apparent meaning. Ibn Ishaq estimated it: they both went back to their father quickly, and their habit had been to be slow in watering, so they told him what had happened with the man who had watered for them. Their father then ordered the elder of his two daughters, and it is said the younger, to invite him, so she came in the manner described in this verse. It is narrated that the name of one of them was (Layya) and the other (Safra). It is also narrated that the name of the wife of the Prophet of God Musa, peace be upon him, was (Safurah), and it is said her name was (Suriyya). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he married him to the elder. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he married him to the younger, and al-Tha'labi and Makki mentioned it through the route of Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him. al-Naqqash said: they were twins, and the first was born half a day before the other.

His words "walking" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "one of the two." His words "shyly" mean: modest, having covered her face with the edge of her garment. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: she was not a bold, forward woman who goes out and in.

People differed about the man who invited Musa, who he was. The majority said he was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and the two women were his daughters. al-Hasan said he was the nephew of Shu'ayb, and his name was Tharwan. Ibn Abi 'Ubayda said: Yathrun. It was also said he was a righteous man, not related to Shu'ayb by lineage. It was also said that the two women were sent by their paternal uncle, and he was the owner of the sheep and the one who gave them in marriage, but the uncle was referred to as "father" in the whole matter since he held his position. It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, was brought the message, he responded and went following her to her father. Then a wind blew and pressed her garment against her body, describing her buttocks, so Musa, peace be upon him, was reluctant to look at her. He said to her: "Walk behind me and guide me on the way." She understood this from him and described him as trustworthy. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.

Musa, peace be upon him, then arrived at the one who had invited him, and related to him his affair from beginning to end. So he comforted him with his words: "Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people." Madyan was outside the kingdom of Pharaoh. When their conversation ended, the daughter who had gone to him said: "O my father, hire him," and the rest of the verse. When she described him with strength and trustworthiness, her father said to her: "From where did you know this about him?" She said: "As for his strength, it is in lifting the stone; and as for his trustworthiness, it is in his reluctance to look at me at the time the wind blew." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and by Ibn Zayd and others.

The father said to him at that point: "Indeed, I want to marry you," and the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: he married him to the one who had invited him. "Tu'jiru" means "tuthību" (reward). Makki said: in this verse there are distinctive features concerning marriage, among them that he did not specify the wife, did not fix the beginning of the term, made the dower a hire (ijarah), and entered without paying anything in advance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

As for specifying, it seems that it occurred in the second stage of the negotiation, as he first put the matter in general terms and specified afterward. As for mentioning the beginning of the term, there is nothing in the verse requiring its omission; rather it is left unstated, so either they fixed it or it is from the time of the contract. As for marriage by hire, it is evident from the verse, and this is a matter that our law has established, and it operated in the hadith of the man who had nothing except some of the Qur'an. Some scholars held that this is specific to him, and others that it is abrogated. Malik, may God have mercy on him, did not permit marriage by hire, while Ibn Habib and others permitted it, provided the payment reaches the wife.

It is said: from the wording of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, in the wording of contracts of marriage, "Ankihuhu iyyaha" (I marry him to her) became more common than "Ankihuha iyyahu" (I marry her to him), and this is open to objection. Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, made the eight years a condition and left the two years to good manners (muruwwa).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 28–32:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said: "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, let there be no injustice against me. And Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾ ﴿Then when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire from the side of the Mount. He said to his family, "Wait here. Indeed I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾ ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And: "Throw down your staff." And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back fleeing and did not look back. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are among the secure.﴾ ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear. These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed they are a people who are defiantly disobedient."﴾

When Shu'ayb finished speaking, Moses (peace be upon him) repeated it, and he repeated its meaning in order to confirm that the condition was fulfilled in eight years. "Ayyama" is an interrogative governed by "qadaytu", and "ma" is an extra particle for emphasis. The majority read "fa-la 'udwana" with a damma on the 'ayn; Abu Haywa read "fa-la 'idwana" with a kasra on the 'ayn. The meaning is: there is no blame upon me for any word or deed. "Al-Wakil" means the witness who stands over the matter.

Ibn Zayd said: When this marriage was completed between them, Shu'ayb ordered Moses (peace be upon them both) to go to a house of his in which there were staffs, and this staff was among them. It is narrated that the staff leapt to Moses and he took it, and it was the staff of Adam (peace be upon him), and it was of the wood of the myrtle (rayhan). It is narrated that Shu'ayb told him to return it, and he did so, then went to take another, and it leapt to him; he did this a third time. When Shu'ayb saw that, he knew that he was destined for prophethood, so he left it for him. It was also said that he left it for him because he had ordered Moses to leave it, and Moses refused. Shu'ayb said to him: "Let us both reach out to it; whoever it obeys, it is his." Shu'ayb reached out and it became heavy, while Moses reached out and it became light and leapt to him. They knew then that this was a sign of his destiny. 'Ikrimah said: Jibril (peace be upon him) brought the staff to him by night when he set out for Madyan.

His, the Exalted's, saying: "Then when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man from the Christians asked me: "Which of the two terms did Moses fulfil?" I said: "I do not know until I come to the best of the Arabs, meaning Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both)." I came to him and asked him, and he said: "He fulfilled the more complete and fuller of the two, for when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said something, he fulfilled it." I returned and informed the Christian, and he said: "By Allah, this scholar has spoken the truth." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about that, and he informed him that he fulfilled ten years." Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he fulfilled ten, and ten after them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak.

In the narrative of this verse, when Moses (peace be upon him) had fulfilled the term, he wished to travel with his family to Egypt and his people. He had undoubtedly sensed his destiny to prophethood, and he was a zealous man who did not keep company with travelling companions. So on part of his journey, on a dark night, — al-Naqqash said: it was a Friday night — they lost the fire, the tinder failed, they lost the way, and the cold became severe upon them. While he was in that state, he saw a fire, and that was a light from the light of Allah the Exalted, which had become entwined with a tree. Wahb said: it was a thorny climbing plant ('ulayq); Qatadah said: it was a hawthorn ('awsaj); it was also said: a jujube tree (za'rur); it was also said: a samurah tree, as reported by Ibn Mas'ud. "Anasa" means "perceived," and the perception here is by sight. From this same root is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿If you perceive in them maturity of judgement﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and from it is the verse of Hassan:

Look, my friend, at the gate of Jillaq; do you perceive anyone beyond al-Balqa'?

All this occurred on the side of the Mount, which is a known mountain in al-Sham. "Tur" means any mountain; some restricted it to a mountain that produces no vegetation. When Moses saw the fire, he was pleased, and he said to his family: "Stay here, for I have seen a fire" — [where it is] from the road, where is it? "Or a burning brand" — that is, a piece of fire in a large piece of wood with no flame, only an ember; from this is the verse of the poet:

The gatherers of Layla spent the night seeking for her firewood of strong kindling, neither rotten nor crumbly.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I think the original meaning of "jadhwa" is the roots of trees, and desert people kindle them continually, so they are truly "jadhwa." From it is the saying of al-Sulami describing the fire-blaze:

Love of this fire has made me love my friend, and love of the beloveds; but it is less than the beloved.

And I was exchanged after musk and ban for misery, the smoke of the kindling on the head of a white-haired, pale man.

The majority read "jidhwatin" with a kasra on the jim; Hamzah and al-A'mash read "judhwatin" with a damma; 'Asim read "jadhwatin" with a fatha. These are dialectal variants. "Al-salaa" means the heat of the fire, and "tasta'lun" is of the form "tafta'ilun," with the ta' changed to ta'.

When Moses came to that light which he saw, and he was forty years old on that night, he was made a prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated that "he was walking towards that light, and it kept receding from him, while the tree remained fresh and green, until he was called." "Al-shati'" and "al-shatt" both mean the bank of the valley. His saying "al-ayman" may be an adjective of "al-wadi" or of "al-shati'" from "al-yumn" (blessing); it may also be the counterpart of "al-yasar" (left). In that case the bank is described as such only relative to Moses, in facing the direction of the valley's descent, or the reverse; both have been said. The blessing of the spot is what it was singled out for of the signs and lights of Allah the Exalted and His speaking to Moses (peace be upon him). The people pronounce the "ba'" of "buq'a" with a damma; al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read it with a fatha. Abu Zayd said: "I heard from the Arabs: 'This is a good spot (baq'a)' with a fatha on the ba'." His saying, the Exalted, "out of the tree" requires that Moses (peace be upon him) heard what he heard from the direction of the tree, and he heard and perceived it without modality or limitation. His saying, the Exalted, "that O Moses" may be an explanatory "an," or it may be in the accusative position with the preposition dropped. A group read "anni ana Allah" with a fatha on the hamza of "inni."

Then Allah the Exalted commanded him to throw down his staff, and he threw it down; it became a great serpent, with the agitation of a jann, which is a small snake, so it combined the terror of a large serpent with the vigour of a jann. Another group said: rather, "jann" applies to both small and large, and the whole staff was likened to a jann only in its agitation. Moses (peace be upon him) turned away fleeing in terror from it. "And he did not return" means he did not come back on his heels from his turning away. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said to him: "O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are among the secure." This is the granting of security by Allah the Exalted to him. Then He commanded him to insert his hand into his bosom, which is the opening of the robe through which a person's head emerges. It is narrated that the sleeve of the robe was extremely tight, so there was no opening for him to insert his hand except through his bosom. "Usluk" means "enter," and from it is the verse of the poet:

Until they drew the hide from them into a tanned skin of the offspring of the she-camel who roams the horizons.

His, the Exalted's, saying: "without harm" means without sickness or the like. It is narrated that his hand would shine as if it were a piece of the sun.

His, the Exalted's, saying: "and draw your arm close to your side against fear" — Mujahid and Ibn Zayd held that this is metaphorical and figurative, and that He commanded him to resolve upon what he was commanded, as the Arabs say: "Tighten your belt, and bind your heart," meaning: exert yourself in your matter and leave off fear. This was because his fear and terror had multiplied in more than one situation; so said Abu 'Ali. His, the Exalted's, saying: "These two are proofs" — Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it refers to the staff and the hand.

I came to him and asked him, and he said: "He fulfilled the more complete and fuller of the two, for when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said something, he fulfilled it." I returned and informed the Christian, and he said: "By Allah, this scholar has spoken the truth." Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he fulfilled ten, and ten after them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I killed a man among them, so I fear they will kill me. And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me as a supporter (ridʼ), to confirm me. Indeed I fear they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said: "We shall strengthen your arm with your brother, and We shall give you both authority, so they shall not reach you. With Our signs, you two and whoever follows you shall be the victors."﴾ ﴿So when Musa came to them with Our clear signs, they said: "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers."﴾ ﴿And Musa said: "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and who will have the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay, and make for me a lofty tower that I may look upon the god of Musa, though indeed I think him among the liars."﴾ ﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land without right, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us.﴾

Musa, peace be upon him, had been tested with fears, so he asked for his arm to be strengthened by his brother Harun, because he was eloquent in speech and gentle in character. The majority of reciters read "ridʼan" (رِدْءًا) with a hamza. Nafi' alone read "ridan" (رِدًّا) with tanwin on the dal without hamza, and this is also the reading of Abu Ja'far. This is by way of lightening the form of "ridʼ" (رِدْءٌ). The ridʼ is the helper who assists and on whom one leans in the matter. A group held that it derives from the meaning of increase, as the poet said:

؎ And a spear-shaft of Khatt, as though its knots were the seeds of the qasb plant, had multiplied (ardā) a cubit upon ten.

(p-593) This is according to omitting the hamza, and its form being fa'l.

The majority of reciters read "yuṣaddiqnī" (يُصَدِّقْنِي) with jazm, in response to the imperative "arsilhu" (أرْسِلْهُ). 'Asim alone read "yuṣaddiqunī" (يُصَدِّقُنِي), meaning "confirming me", so it is an attribute of "ridʼ" or a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

"Shadd al-'adud" (شَدُّ العَضُدِ) is a metaphor for support and empowerment. Al-Hasan read "'ududaka" (عُضُدَكَ) with a damma on the ʿayn, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a fatha on the ʿayn and the ḍād. "Sultan" means proof. His saying "with Our signs" may be connected either to "We shall give you" or to "they shall not reach you," with the bāʾ being causative; or it may be connected to "the victors," meaning you will overcome by Our signs. "Signs" here means his miracles, peace be upon him.

When they denied him and accused him of magic, Musa, peace be upon him, came close to his argument, and their denial troubled him, so he referred the matter to Allah and relied upon what Allah the Exalted would manifest concerning them, and he threatened them with the retribution of Allah the Exalted upon them. The majority read "takūnu lahu" (تَكُونُ لَهُ) with a ta, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yakūnu" (يَكُونُ) with a ya, in the masculine, since the "ʿāqibah" is equivalent to the outcome.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. "Nabadhnāhum" (نَبَذْناهُمْ) means: We cast them away. From it comes "nabdh al-nawāh" (throwing away a date pit). From it is the saying of the poet:

"I looked at its title and cast it away, as you cast away a worn-out sandal from your sandals."

The people of Pharaoh, although they travelled to the sea and entered it by their own choice, what gathered them there of the preordained decree [and their drowning in the sea] is God the Exalted's casting them away into it. "Al-yamm" (اليَمُّ) is the Sea of Qulzum (Red Sea) according to the view of most people, while a group said their drowning was in the Nile of Egypt. The first view is more well known.

"Al-maqbūḥīn" (المَقْبُوحِينَ): those whose entire affair is ugly, in their speech toward them and their deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are those who were made ugly by blackened faces and blue eyes. "Yawm" (يَوْمَ) is a fronted adverbial complement (ẓarf muqaddam).

The purpose of this information is to set an example for the Quraysh through what preceded in other nations. A group said: the verse implies that the sending down of the Torah to Moses was after Allah, the Exalted, lifted the punishment from the nations, so He did not punish any nation after the Torah was sent down, except the town that was transformed into apes, as has been narrated.

His saying "baṣā'ir" (بَصائِرَ) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: clear paths that guide. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that they might remember﴾ means: as a hope, and whatever hope it gives of expectation. The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. So look at how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as insight for the people, guidance and mercy, that they might remember.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 28, verses 44–46:

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses, nor were you among the witnesses.﴾ ﴿But We brought into being generations, and life grew long for them. Nor were you dwelling among the people of Madyan, reciting Our verses to them, but We were the ones who sent (messengers).﴾ ﴿You were not on the side of the Mount when We called out, but (you were sent) as a mercy from your Lord, so that you might warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they might remember.﴾

The meaning: O Muhammad, you were not present for these unseen matters that We inform you of, but they reached you through Our revelation. That is, it was necessary for them to hasten to believe in you. However, time lengthened over the generations that We brought into being, age after age, so their intellects declined, and their ignorance and misguidance became firmly established.

"Qada'na" means: We executed and carried out. "Al-amr" refers to the Torah. A group said: it refers to what Allah, blessed and exalted, made known to Him about the matter of Muhammad ﷺ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good interpretation, one with which what follows, His saying "But We brought into being generations," fits well.

"Al-thawi" means: the one who resides. His saying "You were not on the side of the Mount" means: at the time the Torah was sent down to Musa. His saying "when We called out" has been narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that "he was called out to on that day from the sky: 'O community of Muhammad, I have answered you before you called upon Me, and I have forgiven you before you asked Me.' Then Musa, peace be upon him, asked to be among the community of Muhammad ﷺ."

So the meaning is: when We called out by Your command, and We informed you of your prophethood. His saying "mercy" is in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). His saying "but" (wa-lakin) means: We made you, and We executed Your command long ago, as a mercy from your Lord. That is, the meaning may be: but We informed you as a mercy from Us toward you and as a bounty. The reciters read "rahmatan" with the accusative, and 'Isa read "rahmatun" with the nominative.

By "the people" who "had not received a warner" he means his contemporaries among the Arabs. The rest of the verse is clear. Al-Tabari said: "The meaning of His saying 'when We called out' is that those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet whom they find written (in their scriptures)" (Q. al-A'raf 7:157), and so on, to the end of the verse.
