Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 47–50:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Had it not been that a misfortune should afflict them for what their hands have sent forth, and they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?"﴾ ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?" Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, "Two works of magic supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah which is better guidance than these two, that I may follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿And if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

"Al-muṣība" (the misfortune): a punishment in this world for their disbelief. The response to "law-lā" (had it not been) is omitted, its implied meaning being: "We would not have sent the messengers." His saying, "But when the truth came to them," means: the Qur'an and Muhammad (ﷺ). The statement that the Quraysh made, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?", was from the teaching of the Jews to them; they said to them, "Why does he not bring a clear sign like the staff, the hand, the lifting of the mountain, and other things?" So Allah, exalted is He, turned their words back upon them and made them realise that what had befallen those (earlier people) with those signs was like what had befallen these people with this one. Thus the pronoun in His saying, "they disbelieve," refers to the Jews.

The majority read "sāḥirān" (two sorcerers), and what is meant by them is Moses and Aaron, as said by Mujāhid; al-Ḥasan said: Moses and Jesus; and Ibn 'Abbās said: Moses and Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Ḥasan also said: Jesus and Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace. The first is more apparent. 'Āṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "siḥrān" (two works of magic), and what is meant by them is the Torah and the Gospel, said 'Ikrima; and Ibn 'Abbās said: the Torah and the Furqan. Ibn Mas'ud read "siḥrān ẓāhharā" (two works of magic that support each other), and this is the reading of Ṭalḥa and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that by "what was given to Moses" he means the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) which is in the Torah, as if he is saying: and what do they seek by asking that he be given the like of what was given to Moses, when they have already disbelieved, in denying you, in what was given to Moses, peace be upon him, of the news about you? And they said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both." His saying, the Exalted, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both," supports this interpretation. "Tazāharā" (supporting each other) means: they cooperated.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah"﴾ and what follows is an argument which Allah commanded him to declare openly, meaning: you, O deniers of these books which contain the command to acts of worship and noble character, which forbid disbelief and blameworthy traits, and for which Allah, exalted is He, promised great reward, if your denial is for some reason, then bring a Book from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that gives better guidance than the guidance of these, and I will follow it along with you. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾ — and He already knew that they would not respond — in the sense of clarifying the corruption of their state; and the form of the syllogism is: "because they are followers of their desires." Then the Exalted marvelled at following desire without guidance and without a clear purpose, and established this by way of explanation, meaning: no one is more astray than him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 56–58:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ ﴿And they say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land." Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿And how many a township We destroyed which had exulted in its livelihood! Those are their dwellings, which have not been inhabited after them, except a little. And We are the inheritors.﴾

Most of the exegetes agreed that His saying, ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾, was revealed concerning Abu Talib, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Musayyab, and others said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon him while he was in the throes of death, and said to him: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I will testify for you before Allah.' In his presence were 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah and Abu Jahl, may Allah curse them both. They said to him: 'Do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O Abu Talib?' He said to him: 'O Muhammad, were it not that I fear that my sons will be reproached for it after me, I would have gladdened your eye by it.' Then Abu Talib said: 'I am upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib and the elders.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was grieved and left him, and Abu Talib died upon his disbelief. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾, as an indication concerning Abu Talib."

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿And they say﴾, refers to the Quraysh. Ibn Mas'ud said: the one who spoke this among them was al-Harith ibn Nawfal. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 59–61:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿Your Lord would never destroy the mother-towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of this worldly life and its adornment; but what is with God is better and more lasting. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and who will encounter it, like one whom We have given the enjoyment of the worldly life and then, on the Day of Resurrection, he will be among those brought forward [for punishment]?﴾

If the destruction of towns is taken in an absolute sense, in every age, then "their mother-town" in this place refers to the greatest and most excellent of them, which is in the position of Makkah in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). And even if Makkah is the mother of all towns, since it was the first place of the earth to be created, and since the House is in it, the meaning of the verse is that God, blessed and exalted, establishes the proof against His servants through the messengers, so He does not punish except after a warning, and after the people of the towns have persisted in wrongdoing and transgression. Wrongdoing here (ẓulm) comprises disbelief, sins, and neglect in striving (jihad), and in sum, placing falsehood in the place of truth.

(p-602) Then God, exalted, addressed the Quraysh, belittling what they used to boast of, namely wealth, sons, and other forms of strength which were not possessed by Muhammad (ﷺ) nor by those who believed in him. God informed the Quraysh that this is the transient enjoyment of the world, and that the Hereafter, with its bounties which God has prepared for these believers, is better and more lasting. Then He rebuked them by His saying: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ The majority read "ya'qilūn" (they reason) with the yā' (y), while Abū 'Amr alone read "ta'qilūn" (you reason) with the tā' (t) at the beginning. This is also the reading of al-A'raj, al-Hasan and 'Isa.

Then He increased their rebuke with His saying: ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise﴾ and so on. His saying ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise﴾ in its meaning encompasses the whole world, but people differed about who was meant by its revelation. Mujahid said: the one promised the good is Muhammad (ﷺ), and his opposite is Abu Jahl, may God curse him. Mujahid also said: it was revealed concerning Hamza, may God be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. Qatada said: it was revealed concerning the believer and the disbeliever, just as its meaning is general.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Its revelation being general is clearly consistent with what precedes it of the rebuke of the Quraysh.

And ﴿among those brought forward﴾ means: in the punishment of God, the Exalted, as said by Mujahid and Qatada. The word "muhdarīn" (those brought forward) indicates driving and dragging. Talha read "amman wa'adnāhu" without the fā' (fa), and Masruq read "afaman wa'adnāhu ni'matun minnā fahuwa lāqīhi" (Is one to whom We have made a promise of a bounty from Us, and he will encounter it...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 62–64:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿Those against whom the Word has been justified will say, "Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray; we led them astray just as we went astray. We disown them before You; they did not worship us."﴾ ﴿And it will be said, "Call upon your partners," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!﴾

The estimated reading (al-taqdir) is: "Remember the Day." This calling (al-nida') may be through an intermediary, and it may be otherwise. The pronoun in "yunadi" (He calls) refers to the worshippers of idols, and the address is to Quraysh. His saying "Where" (ayna) is in the manner of rebuke and reproach. His saying "My partners" (shuraka'iya) means: according to your claim and your assertion.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Since this question silences them and humiliates them, it seems that it does not concern the general body of disbelievers, except for those who misled them, the notables and leaders among them, and the misleading devils. It is as if this misleading group came to the disbelievers knowing that the Word against them had been realised and that the word of punishment had been decreed. Yet they hoped to disown those disbelieving followers, so they said, "Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray, just as we ourselves went astray, through our own exertion and theirs." They wanted their following of us, and they loved disbelief just as we loved it. So we disown them before You, and they did not worship us; they only worshipped others than us.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interrogation therefore includes all the disbelievers, and those who answer are all the misleaders, each one a caller to disbelief: from among the devils, the jinn; and from among humans, the chiefs, the leaders and the lords.

The majority of readers recite "ghawayna" (we went astray) with a fatha on the waw. It is said that "ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi" (the man went astray) is with a kasra on the waw. It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim that they recited "ghawina" with a kasra on the waw.

Then He, blessed and exalted, informed that it will be said to the disbelieving idol-worshippers, who had believed them to be gods: ﴿Call upon your partners﴾, meaning the idols which you used to claim were partners to God. He attributed the partners to them because that designation was by their claim and assertion. This statement is the basis of the principle of specification: He attributed the partners to them, then informed that they called upon them, but there was nothing among the inanimate things that could respond, and the disbelievers saw the punishment. As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾, al-Zajjaj and other exegetes held that the answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, its estimated form being: "it would not have befallen them the punishment," or: "they would not have been worshipping idols in the world." Thus, on this interpretation, there is in the statement an expression of regret over them. This is possible with our estimate of the answer as "they would not have been worshipping idols," while with our estimate of the answer as "the punishment would not have befallen them," it is a favour from Us. Another group said that "law" is connected to what precedes it, the estimated sense being: "so they wished that they had been guided."

Yet they hoped to disown those disbelieving followers, so they said, "Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray, just as we ourselves went astray, through our own exertion and theirs." They wanted their following of us, and they loved disbelief just as we loved it. So we disown them before You, and they did not worship us; they only worshipped others than us.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interrogation therefore includes all the disbelievers, and those who answer are all the misleaders, each one a caller to disbelief: from among the devils, the jinn; and from among humans, the chiefs, the leaders and the lords.

The majority of readers recite "ghawayna" (we went astray) with a fatha on the waw. It is said that "ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi" (the man went astray) is with a kasra on the waw. It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim that they recited "ghawina" with a kasra on the waw.

Then He, blessed and exalted, informed that it will be said to the disbelieving idol-worshippers, who had believed them to be gods: ﴿Call upon your partners﴾, meaning the idols which you used to claim were partners to God. He attributed the partners to them because that designation was by their claim and assertion. This statement is the basis of the principle of specification: He attributed the partners to them, then informed that they called upon them, but there was nothing among the inanimate things that could respond, and the disbelievers saw the punishment. As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿If only they had been guided!﴾, al-Zajjaj and other exegetes held that the answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, its estimated form being: "it would not have befallen them the punishment," or: "they would not have been worshipping idols in the world." Thus, on this interpretation, there is in the statement an expression of regret over them. This is possible with our estimate of the answer as "they would not have been worshipping idols," while with our estimate of the answer as "the punishment would not have befallen them," it is a favour from Us. Another group said that "law" is connected to what precedes it, the estimated sense being: "so they wished that they had been guided."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 28, verses 65–68:**

The Exalted said:

﴿On the Day He calls to them and says, "What answer did you give the messengers?"﴾ ﴿Then the news will be obscured from them that Day, and they will not question one another.﴾ ﴿But as for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, perhaps he will be among the successful.﴾ ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. It is not for them to choose. Glory be to Allah, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

This call, like the first, may involve an intermediary from among the angels. This call is also addressed to the disbelievers, confronting them with what they answered the messengers who invited them to Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Then the news will be obscured from them﴾ means: the matters will be darkened, so they will find no report to give that would bring them salvation. The verb is cast in the past tense (*al-madi*) to affirm that its occurrence is certain and fixed. The past tense is the most certain of verb forms, so it is used in place of the future to strengthen the certainty and reality of the event. Its meaning is that its aspects became dark. al-Aʿmash read *fa-ʿummiyat* (with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn and a *shadda* on the mīm). It is reported in some hadith: "Allah was in ʿamāʾ (a cloud/void)," and that was before He created the lights and the rest of the creatures. *Al-anbāʾ* is the plural of *naba'* (news). The Exalted's words ﴿and they will not question one another﴾ mean, as Mujahid and others said: by kinship and lineage, which in this world is the means by which people ask one another; for they have become certain that none of them has any stratagem or station. It is also possible that it means they will not question one another about the reports, because all of them are certain that they have no proof.

Then the Exalted singled out from among the disbelievers those who repented of their disbelief, believed in Allah and His messengers, and acted with piety. He expressed hope (*rajjā*) that they would attain their desire and remain in everlasting bliss. Many scholars said: "*ʿasā*" (perhaps) from Allah is obligatory.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good opinion of Allah, the Exalted, befitting His grace and generosity. What follows from *ʿasā* is that it expresses hope (*tarajjī*), not obligation. In the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Perhaps his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

As for the Exalted's words ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾ and the rest of the verse, it was said that its cause was what Quraysh said in wonder at the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, and the saying of some of them: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. So this verse was revealed because of those disputes, and Allah, the Exalted, answered them. He informed that He creates from among His servants and the rest of His creatures what He wills, and that He chooses for His message whom He wills and places in it the benefit. Then He negated that the choice belongs to people in this matter or similar ones. This is the saying of a group of exegetes, who said that *mā* is a negative particle, meaning: the choice does not belong to them instead of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted. The verse then resembles the Exalted's words: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36].

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that it means: Allah, the Exalted, chooses the religions and the laws, and it is not for them to choose to incline toward idols and the like in worship. This interpretation is supported by His words: ﴿Glory be to Allah, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

al-Tabari held that *mā* in His words ﴿and chooses what﴾ is an object (*mafʿūlah*). He said: the meaning is that the disbelievers used to choose the best of their wealth for their idols, so Allah, the Exalted, informed that choosing belongs to Him alone. He creates and chooses from among the messengers and the laws what is good for people, not as they choose for themselves what is not theirs, and do what they were not commanded to do.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

al-Tabari made excuses for the *raf*ʿ (nominative vowelling) on which the readers unanimously agreed in the Exalted's words ﴿It is not for them to choose﴾, with statements that do not amount to anything. People have refuted him on this. He also reported from al-Farra' that al-Qasim ibn Maʿn recited to him the verse of ʿAntara:

*Is it because of Sumayya that the tears of the eye flow?*
*If only that (one) had been a kindness from you before today.*

He linked the verse with this line. The reported version of the line is: "*law anna dhā*" (if that one). But according to what al-Qasim related, it is plausible in ʿAntara's line that the pronoun be a dummy pronoun of the matter and affair (*ḍamīr al-amr wa-l-shaʾn*). As for the verse, this cannot be, since the clause following it contains an omitted element. All of this is open to scrutiny.

The pause (*waqf*) according to the view of the majority of people is at His words ﴿and chooses﴾; according to the view of al-Tabari, one does not pause there.

It appears to me that *mā* may be an object if we take *kāna* as a complete verb (*tāmmah*), meaning that Allah, the Exalted, chooses every existing thing, and nothing happens except by His permission. His words, blessed and exalted, ﴿It is not for them to choose﴾ form a resumptive independent clause (*jumlah mustaʾnafah*), whose meaning is to enumerate the blessing upon them in Allah's choosing for them, if they accept and understand.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 69–73:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And He is Allah; there is no god except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [life], and to Him is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you light? Then will you not hear?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Then will you not see?"﴾ ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

In these verses, the Exalted mentions matters for which the intellect of every person created with a natural disposition (fitrah) testifies that the idols have no share in them. Among them is the knowledge of what is in the souls and what passes through the thoughts. "Yukinnu" (تُكِنُّ) means "conceals," and Ibn Muhaysin read "takunnu" (تَكُنُّ) with a fatha on the ta and a damma on the kaf. He expressed the heart by "the breasts" (al-sudur) since it is contained within them. The meaning of the verse is that Allah, the Exalted, knows the secret and the public.

Then He singled Himself out for divinity (uluhiyyah) and negated it from anything else, and informed that praise belongs to Him in this world and the Hereafter, since He possesses the attributes that necessitate that, and judgment belongs to Him. And it, in this place, means the decision and determination of affairs. Then the Exalted informed of the return to Him and the gathering (hashr).

Then the Exalted instructed His Prophet to make them stand before the matter of the night and the day, and what Allah, the Exalted, bestowed in them of benefits and conveniences, and to make them stand before His favour, the Exalted, in the alternation of night and day, and that if He extended one of them perpetually, they would not find anyone who could bring the other. "Sarmad" (السَرْمَدُ), concerning things, means that which is lasting and does not cease. A group, which is the majority, read "biḍiyā'in" (بِضِياءٍ) with a ya; Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Qunbul, read "biḍi'ā'in" (بِضِئاءٍ) with two hamzas, and Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) regarded it as weak. Then the Exalted mentioned the division of night and day into rest and the seeking of bounty through walking and activity. This is the predominant case regarding night and day, so He enumerated the blessing by the most common instance; and if one finds someone who rests by day and seeks Allah's bounty by night, that is a rare anomaly which is not taken into account. Some people said: the saying of the Exalted, "He made for you the night and the day," is only an expression for time, as if He did not intend a division; that is, in this time which is night and day, rest and the seeking of bounty take place.

His saying, "and perhaps," means, from the viewpoint of humans: whoever perceives this gentleness and kindness sees that it necessarily calls for gratitude.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 69–73:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And He is Allah; there is no god except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [life], and to Him is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you light? Then will you not hear?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Then will you not see?"﴾ ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

In these verses, the Exalted mentions matters for which the intellect of every person created with a natural disposition (fitrah) testifies that the idols have no share in them. Among them is the knowledge of what is in the souls and what passes through the thoughts. "Yukinnu" (تُكِنُّ) means "conceals," and Ibn Muhaysin read "takunnu" (تَكُنُّ) with a fatha on the ta and a damma on the kaf. He expressed the heart by "the breasts" (al-sudur) since it is contained within them. The meaning of the verse is that Allah, the Exalted, knows the secret and the public.

Then He singled Himself out for divinity (uluhiyyah) and negated it from anything else, and informed that praise belongs to Him in this world and the Hereafter, since He possesses the attributes that necessitate that, and judgment belongs to Him. And it, in this place, means the decision and determination of affairs. Then the Exalted informed of the return to Him and the gathering (hashr).

Then the Exalted instructed His Prophet to make them stand before the matter of the night and the day, and what Allah, the Exalted, bestowed in them of benefits and conveniences, and to make them stand before His favour, the Exalted, in the alternation of night and day, and that if He extended one of them perpetually, they would not find anyone who could bring the other. "Sarmad" (السَرْمَدُ), concerning things, means that which is lasting and does not cease. A group, which is the majority, read "biḍiyā'in" (بِضِياءٍ) with a ya; Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Qunbul, read "biḍi'ā'in" (بِضِئاءٍ) with two hamzas, and Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) regarded it as weak. Then the Exalted mentioned the division of night and day into rest and the seeking of bounty through walking and activity. This is the predominant case regarding night and day, so He enumerated the blessing by the most common instance; and if one finds someone who rests by day and seeks Allah's bounty by night, that is a rare anomaly which is not taken into account. Some people said: the saying of the Exalted, "He made for you the night and the day," is only an expression for time, as if He did not intend a division; that is, in this time which is night and day, rest and the seeking of bounty take place.

His saying, "and perhaps," means, from the viewpoint of humans: whoever perceives this gentleness and kindness sees that it necessarily calls for gratitude.

The passage is from Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 74–75:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw out from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and what they used to invent will be lost to them.﴾

The implied phrase is: "Mention the Day He calls to them." This idea is repeated for emphasis and warning. This calling takes place when everything that the Most Merciful promised through the tongues of the messengers becomes manifest: the obligation of mercy for one people, the punishment for others, the submission of every tyrant, and the humbling before the might of the Lord of the worlds. At that point, the rebuke of the disbelievers begins, and God the Exalted says to them, "Where are My partners?" in the sense of reproach.

Then the Blessed and Exalted One informs that on that day He will bring forth from every nation a witness who distinguishes it from the people. This is "al-nazc" (extraction), meaning that one of two things is distinguished and one is extracted from the other. Mujahid said that by "al-shahid" (the witness) is meant the one who bears witness against his nation. Al-Rummani said: it has been said that it means the just and righteous ones from among the nations.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

They are the bearers of the proof, who are never absent from any era. "Al-shahid" according to this interpretation is a generic noun (ism al-jins). In this place there is an ellipsis indicated by the apparent meaning, its estimated form being: the witness testifies against the nation, to its good and its bad, and so punishment becomes due for whoever disbelieved. They will be told, by way of "istibra' al-hujja" (testing the proof) and giving them an excuse in the argument: "Bring your proof," meaning your proof for what you were upon in the world, if you have any. Then they will be left helpless, and they will know that the truth belongs to Him, glory be to Him, in His punishing them. What they were following in the world of fabricated falsehood and lies in their saying about the idols, "These are gods," and in their denial of the messengers, and other things, will be revealed to them. And from this verse was derived the saying of the judge when he intends to pass judgment: "Has any proof remained for you?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 76–77:

His the Exalted, the Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he tyrannized over them. And We had given him of the treasures such that its keys would weigh heavily upon a band of strong men, when his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾

Qarun: a non-Arabic name, and therefore it is not declined. People differed regarding Qarun's kinship to Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn Ishaq said he was his paternal uncle; Ibn Juraij and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said he was his cousin, and this is the more well known view. It was also said he was his maternal cousin. He was, by consensus, a man from the Children of Israel who had believed in Musa, memorised the Torah, and was among the most proficient of people in it. He was among the devout believers in the company of Musa, peace be upon him. Then pride and self-admiration overtook him, and he tyrannized over his people in various forms of oppression. Among these was his disbelief in Musa and his belittling of him, and his demand that Musa make something for him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he went to a prostitute of beauty and said to her, "I will treat you well and protect you among my family, on condition that you come to an assembly of the Children of Israel at my place and say, 'O Qarun, relieve me of the matter of Musa, for he is pursuing me in my soul.'" The woman came, and when she stood before the assembly, Allah the Exalted caused her to repent. She said, "O Children of Israel, Qarun said to me such and such," and she exposed him in the entire account. And Allah, by His power, cleared His Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, of the accusation. It was also said: rather, the woman said that about Musa; when the news reached him, he brought the woman before a gathering of the Children of Israel, and she said, "O Prophet of Allah, I lied about you, and it was only Qarun who drove me to this statement." Among his oppression was that he lengthened his garments by a span over the garments of the people; this was related by Shahr ibn Hawshab, along with other things that issue from one whose belief has become corrupt. He was among the greatest of people in wealth, and his wealth was called treasures because he refrained from paying zakat. Because of this, Musa, peace be upon him, took him as an enemy at the beginning of his enmity.

As for "al-mafatih" (the keys): their apparent meaning is that they are the things by which one opens, though it is possible that by them is meant the storehouses and large containers; this was said by al-Dahhak, because "miftah" (key) in the speech of the Arabs means a storehouse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The exegetes have said much regarding Qarun. It is related from Khaytham that he said: "We find written in the Injil: 'The keys of Qarun were made of camel hide, and each key was half a span long, and they were a load for sixty mules or camels, each key being a treasure.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Other reports close to this have also been related, but all of that is weak, and reasoning testifies to its corruption. Who would have been distinguishing some of them from others? What is the purpose of this? And is it possible that all of them return to what can be counted and carried with ease? According to this, it would have been necessary for "mafatih" to be written with a *ya*, which is the reading of al-A'mash. What seems correct is: either the keys are of iron or the like, and on this basis "they weigh heavily upon a band" makes sense, since they were numerous because of the multitude of his storehouses; or "al-mafatih" means the storehouses. Abu Salih said: his treasuries were carried by forty mules.

As for His saying "tanu'" (weigh heavily): its meaning is "to rise with difficulty," and from this is the verse of the poet describing an archer:

"Until, when his joints came together and his shoulder blade drooped on the left side..."

The proper way to put it is that the band weighs heavily under the keys that burden them. Many of the interpreters have also said that this is what is meant, but it is an inversion (qalb), as the Arabs often do. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I have ransomed myself and my wealth with his self, and I spare nothing except what I am able to bear."

And the words of another:

"You ride horses with no mercy between them, and the spears are made to suffer by the red-haired (or reddish) horsemen."

This verse offers no proof, since it can be read in its literal sense; so reflect on it. From this also is the verse of another:

"You were not, in the war of the middle-aged, one who is covered over, when the heat of its fire ignited its stubble."

Sibawayh and al-Khalil said: the estimate is "to make the band weigh heavily," so in place of that the verb is transitive by means of the preposition, as you say: "the load weighed heavily" (nā'a al-himl) and "I made it weigh heavily" (anta'tuhu), and "I made it weigh heavily upon the camel" (nu'tu bihi), meaning "I made it bear down." The Arabs say: "the load weighed heavily on the camel" when it burdened it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "tanu'" is attributed to the keys figuratively, because they rise with difficulty when that which rises with them does so under strain. This is consistent with their saying, "the load weighed heavily on the camel," and similar expressions, so reflect on it.

People differed concerning "the band," how many it is. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: three. Qatada said: the band is from ten to forty. Mujahid said: fifteen. It was also said: eleven, based on the brothers of Yusuf. It was said: forty.

Badil ibn Maysara recited "la-yanu'" with a *ya*, and Abu al-Fath explained it on the basis that he read "mafatihahu" as a plural. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Badil ibn Maysara read "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so on this basis the explanation of Abu al-Fath is unnecessary.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿when his people said to him﴾ is connected to His saying "tyrannized," and they forbade him from the insolent exultation, which is the absorption and dissolution of the soul, arrogance and self-admiration. And "does not love" in this place is an attribute of action, because it is a matter that has already occurred, so it is impossible to return it to will; rather, it means He does not bestow upon them His blessing and does not grant them His mercy. Then they advised him to seek with his wealth the pleasure of Allah and the Hereafter. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and do not forget your share of the world﴾ has been differently interpreted by the commentators. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your worldly life, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world; so a person's share is his life and his righteous deed, and he should not neglect it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, the whole speech is intense admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: its meaning is: (p-613) do not also neglect your portion of your worldly good by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, and by looking to the outcome of your worldly life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, the speech is about gentleness toward him and the rectifying of the matter he desires, and this is something that must be employed with one being admonished, out of fear of aversion caused by severity. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: put forward the surplus and keep back what suffices you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. Al-Tha'labi related that it was said: they meant by his share the shroud.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a connected admonition, as if they said: do not forget that you will leave all your wealth except your share, which is the shroud. A similar statement is the verse of the poet:

"Your share of all that you gather throughout time is two garments in which you are wrapped, and perfume."

His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ is a command to give to the needy and those in want. The rest of the verse is clear.

Other reports close to this have also been related, but all of that is weak, and reasoning testifies to its corruption. Who would have been distinguishing some of them from others? What is the purpose of this? And is it possible that all of them return to what can be counted and carried with ease? According to this, it would have been necessary for "mafatih" to be written with a *ya*, which is the reading of al-A'mash. What seems correct is: either the keys are of iron or the like, and on this basis "they weigh heavily upon a band" makes sense, since they were numerous because of the multitude of his storehouses; or "al-mafatih" means the storehouses. Abu Salih said: his treasuries were carried by forty mules.

As for His saying "tanu'" (weigh heavily): its meaning is "to rise with difficulty," and from this is the verse of the poet describing an archer:

"Until, when his joints came together and his shoulder blade drooped on the left side..."

The proper way to put it is that the band weighs heavily under the keys that burden them. Many of the interpreters have also said that this is what is meant, but it is an inversion (qalb), as the Arabs often do. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I have ransomed myself and my wealth with his self, and I spare nothing except what I am able to bear."

And the words of another:

"You ride horses with no mercy between them, and the spears are made to suffer by the red-haired (or reddish) horsemen."

This verse offers no proof, since it can be read in its literal sense; so reflect on it. From this also is the verse of another:

"You were not, in the war of the middle-aged, one who is covered over, when the heat of its fire ignited its stubble."

Sibawayh and al-Khalil said: the estimate is "to make the band weigh heavily," so in place of that the verb is transitive by means of the preposition, as you say: "the load weighed heavily" (nā'a al-himl) and "I made it weigh heavily" (anta'tuhu), and "I made it weigh heavily upon the camel" (nu'tu bihi), meaning "I made it bear down." The Arabs say: "the load weighed heavily on the camel" when it burdened it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "tanu'" is attributed to the keys figuratively, because they rise with difficulty when that which rises with them does so under strain. This is consistent with their saying, "the load weighed heavily on the camel," and similar expressions, so reflect on it.

People differed concerning "the band," how many it is. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: three. Qatada said: the band is from ten to forty. Mujahid said: fifteen. It was also said: eleven, based on the brothers of Yusuf. It was said: forty.

Badil ibn Maysara recited "la-yanu'" with a *ya*, and Abu al-Fath explained it on the basis that he read "mafatihahu" as a plural. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Badil ibn Maysara read "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so on this basis the explanation of Abu al-Fath is unnecessary.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿when his people said to him﴾ is connected to His saying "tyrannized," and they forbade him from the insolent exultation, which is the absorption and dissolution of the soul, arrogance and self-admiration. And "does not love" in this place is an attribute of action, because it is a matter that has already occurred, so it is impossible to return it to will; rather, it means He does not bestow upon them His blessing and does not grant them His mercy. Then they advised him to seek with his wealth the pleasure of Allah and the Hereafter. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and do not forget your share of the world﴾ has been differently interpreted by the commentators. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your worldly life, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world; so a person's share is his life and his righteous deed, and he should not neglect it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, the whole speech is intense admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: its meaning is: (p-613) do not also neglect your portion of your worldly good by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, and by looking to the outcome of your worldly life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, the speech is about gentleness toward him and the rectifying of the matter he desires, and this is something that must be employed with one being admonished, out of fear of aversion caused by severity. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: put forward the surplus and keep back what suffices you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. Al-Tha'labi related that it was said: they meant by his share the shroud.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a connected admonition, as if they said: do not forget that you will leave all your wealth except your share, which is the shroud. A similar statement is the verse of the poet:

"Your share of all that you gather throughout time is two garments in which you are wrapped, and perfume."

His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ is a command to give to the needy and those in want. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 78–79:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿He said, "I have been given it only on knowledge I possess. Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation? And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins."﴾ ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment. Those who desired the worldly life said, "Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is one of great fortune."﴾

The one who spoke was Qarun. When his people admonished him and urged him to fear Allah, Exalted is He, regarding the wealth that He had given him as a bounty from Him to him, pride in his sin took hold of him, so he became self-admiring. He said to them, by way of rejecting them and evading what they had obligated him to: ﴿I have been given it only on knowledge I possess.﴾ His statement carries two possible meanings, and a group of the exegetes said for each of them:

The majority of them said: he claimed that he had knowledge which entitled him to that bounty and likewise the wealth. Then they differed regarding the knowledge to which he alluded, what was it? Some of them said: the knowledge of the Torah and its memorization. They said: this was deception and ostentation. Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: he meant knowledge of trade and the ways of distinguishing wealth, so it was as if he said: "I have been given it by my own perception and my own effort." Ibn al-Musayyib said: he meant the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimya').

Ibn Zayd and others said: he only meant: "I have been given it on knowledge from Allah, Exalted is He, and a specification from Him which chose me for it, so nothing from what you say is binding on me." Then his saying "on my knowledge" (ʿindi) was taken as one says: "in my belief and according to what I see."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On both possibilities together, the Qur'an has drawn attention to his error in his deception, and has countered his inclination by the fact that among the known and established matters of people is that Allah, Exalted is He, has destroyed from the nations, the generations and the kings those who were greater than Qarun in strength and more abundant in gathering, whether in wealth or in retinue. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Did he not know?﴾ indicates that Qarun was filled with knowledge of himself according to his own claim.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is a statement connected in meaning to what precedes it, and the pronoun in "their sins" refers to those among the generations who were destroyed; that is, they were destroyed and no one after them was questioned about their sins; that is, each person is only questioned and punished according to what pertains to him. Another group said: it is a new report about their state on the Day of Resurrection, its meaning being that the criminals will not be questioned about their sins, that is, the angels will not ask about their sins, because they recognize them by their marks of blackness, disfigurement and the like, as in His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41].

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the signs of Allah is what indicates that people will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24], and other than that. And there are verses which indicate that no one will be questioned, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ [al-Rahman: 39], and other than that. It is possible that the verses which establish questioning intend questions of reproach and confirmation, while what is negated intends questions of inquiry out of need to know that matter from those questioned, that is, that this does not occur, because knowledge of them is all-encompassing, and questioning for reproach is not counted.

Then Exalted is He informed that Qarun went out to his people, having displayed his power through clothing, mounts and the adornment of the world. Jabir and Mujahid said: he went out in red garments. Ibn Zayd said: he went out with his entourage in saffron-dyed garments. It was said: in garments of purple (al-urjuwan). It was said other than this. The exegetes exaggerated in specifying and identifying the adornment of Qarun, with what has no soundness, so I have abbreviated it. The remainder of the verse concerning the deception of the ignorant and the foolish among people is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verses 80–82:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness; and none is granted it except the patient."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was not for him any company to aid him against Allah, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.﴾ ﴿And morning came upon those who had wished to be in his position the day before, saying, "Woe! It is that Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it]. Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It is that the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾

He, exalted is He, informed about those who had been given knowledge and recognition of Allah, the Exalted, and of the true obedience due to Him and faith in Him, that they rebuked the ignorant ones who had wished for the condition of Qarun, and guided them to the correct way: that contemplation and wishing belong only to matters of the Hereafter, and that the state of the believing doer who awaits the reward of Allah is better than the state of every person of worldly life.

(p-616) Then He, exalted is He, informed about this inclination and this strength in goodness in religion, that it is not received (lā yulaqqāhā), meaning it is not granted or bestowed except upon the one who is patient in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in restraining the desires of his soul; and this is the sum of all goodness. The pronoun in "yulaqqāhā" refers to something not previously mentioned, but whose meaning is implied by the context; it is like the usage in ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32] and ﴿everyone upon it will perish﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 26]. Al-Tabari said: the pronoun refers to the saying, namely His words ﴿the reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness﴾, meaning: this statement is not received except by the patient, and it is from them that it issues.

It is narrated concerning the swallowing of Qarun and his home that when Musa, peace be upon him, was distressed by Qarun's conduct toward him, his transgression against him, his slander with the matter of the woman, and other of his deeds, he sought refuge with Allah, the Exalted, wept, and asked for help. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "Do not grieve, for I have commanded the earth to obey you concerning Qarun, his household, his close associates and his followers." Musa, peace be upon him, said to the earth: "Seize them." So it seized them up to their knees, and they cried out for help to Musa, "O Musa!" He said, "Seize them," and it took them bit by bit while they called upon him each time, and he kept insisting until the swallowing was complete. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "O Musa, they cried to you for help and you did not show them mercy; had they cried to Me and turned to Me in repentance, I would have had mercy on them and removed what afflicts them." Qatadah and Malik ibn Dinar said: "It was related to us that he is swallowed a stature's height each day, and he will continue sinking until the Day of Resurrection."

"Al-fi'ah" means the supporting group to which a person seeking help turns.

The story of Qarun occurred after their crossing of the sea, because the narrators mentioned that he was among those who had memorised the Torah and used to recite it.

Then He, exalted is He, informed about the condition of those who had wished for his position the day before, and about their regret and their realisation that power and might belong to Allah, the Exalted. His saying "wa-ykaʾanna" (ويكأن): the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil is that "way" (ويْ) is an particle of alerting, separate from "ka-anna" (كأنّ), but in the written text they were joined due to frequent usage. [The meaning is that the people woke up and spoke according to the measure of their knowledge, or they were alerted and it was said to them: "Does it not seem that this is with you thus?"] (p-617) They said, in a manner of wonder and remorse: "Indeed Allah extends provision..."

Abu Hatim and a group of grammarians said: "wayka" is "waylaka" (ويلك), whose lam has been elided and which continued in speech in that form. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"Indeed he has healed my soul and cooled its sickness, the saying of the horsemen: 'Woe to you, 'Antar, advance!'"

So the meaning is: "Woe to you, know that Allah..." and similar to this is the omission of the verb.

A group of grammarians said: "wayka-anna" as a whole, without assuming a separate word, is like your saying: "Did you not see that..."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The separation (of "way") is strengthened by the view of Sibawayh, because it comes with "anna" and with "an", and Sibawayh recited:

"Way, ka-an, he who possesses wealth is made to be envied, and he who becomes poor lives a life of hardship."

(p-618) This verse belongs to Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

Al-A'mash read "lawla man Allah" with the elision of "an", and it is related from him: "lawla minnu" with a raised nun and with idafa to "Allah". The majority read "lakhusifa" with a damma on the kha and a kasra on the sin; 'Asim read with a fatha on the kha and the sin; al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "la-nakhsifa" as if it were an imperfect verb, intending that the earth was affected. It is related from al-Kisa'i that he would pause on "way" and begin with "ka-anna", and it is also related from him that he connected them like the majority. It is related from Abu 'Amr that he would pause on "wayka" and begin with "inna Allah". On this meaning al-Hasan said: "If you wish, say 'wayka anna' or 'wayka inna', with a fatha or a kasra on the hamza; likewise with 'wayka-annahu'."

His saying "wa-ykaʾanna" (ويكأن): the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil is that "way" (ويْ) is an particle of alerting, separate from "ka-anna" (كأنّ), but in the written text they were joined due to frequent usage. [The meaning is that the people woke up and spoke according to the measure of their knowledge, or they were alerted and it was said to them: "Does it not seem that this is with you thus?"] (p-617) They said, in a manner of wonder and remorse: "Indeed Allah extends provision..."

Abu Hatim and a group of grammarians said: "wayka" is "waylaka" (ويلك), whose lam has been elided and which continued in speech in that form. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"Indeed he has healed my soul and cooled its sickness, the saying of the horsemen: 'Woe to you, 'Antar, advance!'"

So the meaning is: "Woe to you, know that Allah..." and similar to this is the omission of the verb.

A group of grammarians said: "wayka-anna" as a whole, without assuming a separate word, is like your saying: "Did you not see that..."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The separation (of "way") is strengthened by the view of Sibawayh, because it comes with "anna" and with "an", and Sibawayh recited:

"Way, ka-an, he who possesses wealth is made to be envied, and he who becomes poor lives a life of hardship."

(p-618) This verse belongs to Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

Al-A'mash read "lawla man Allah" with the elision of "an", and it is related from him: "lawla minnu" with a raised nun and with idafa to "Allah". The majority read "lakhusifa" with a damma on the kha and a kasra on the sin; 'Asim read with a fatha on the kha and the sin; al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "la-nakhsifa" as if it were an imperfect verb, intending that the earth was affected. It is related from al-Kisa'i that he would pause on "way" and begin with "ka-anna", and it is also related from him that he connected them like the majority. It is related from Abu 'Amr that he would pause on "wayka" and begin with "inna Allah". On this meaning al-Hasan said: "If you wish, say 'wayka anna' or 'wayka inna', with a fatha or a kasra on the hamza; likewise with 'wayka-annahu'."

This is a statement from God, the Exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, intended as information for the whole world and as an exhortation to strive in accordance with what the verse contains. This exhortation implies a rebuke of the condition of Qarun (Korah) and his like. The meaning is that the Hereafter has nothing to do with the affair of Qarun; it belongs only to those whose attribute is such-and-such. The blameworthy *'uluw* (haughtiness, exaltation over others), which is oppression and tyranny, is what the Prophet ﷺ referred to when he said: «That is when you wish that your shoelace be better than your brother's shoelace.» *Al-fasad* (corruption) encompasses all forms of evil, and among what the scholars have said about it is that it is taking wealth without right. His saying ﴿and the good end is for the God-fearing﴾ is a separate statement.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him is better than it﴾ means either in this world or in the Hereafter, and it must be one of them. So in describing the reward in the Hereafter as such, it means that whoever does righteousness, for him is something better than the measure which reasoning would require to be equal to that deed. This is on the basis that we take *al-hasanah* (the good deed) in the comparative sense, and in the statement there is an omitted modifier, meaning: from its reward that is equal to it. It is also possible that *min* (from) indicates the starting point, meaning: for him is good according to his good deed and because of it. He, may He be blessed and exalted, informed that the reward for an evil deed is not multiplied, as a favour and mercy from Him.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained for you the Qur'an will surely bring you back to a return﴾ means: He sent it down to you and established it. *Al-fard* (ordaining) originally is a mark made by a tool on wood or the like, so things that are established, fixed and remain resemble that mark. Mujahid said: its meaning is: He gave you the Qur'an. Another group said: in this statement there is an omitted modifier, and the meaning is: He ordained upon you the rulings of the Qur'an.

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿will surely bring you back to a return﴾. The majority of the interpreters said: it means the Hereafter, that is, He will resurrect you after death. So the verse, according to this view, aims at affirming the gathering (of the dead) and informing of its occurrence. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others said: *al-ma'ad* (the return) is Paradise. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and a group said: *al-ma'ad* is death.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the verse, according to this view, is an admonition and a reminder.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid: *al-ma'ad* is Makkah, and this verse was revealed at al-Juhfa, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was about to migrate to Madinah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the verse, according to this view, informs of an unseen matter that became manifest to the community, and gives comfort with a conquest. *Al-ma'ad* is the place to which one returns, and it has become known as the designation for the Day of Resurrection, because it is a return for all.

Al-Tabari, in his interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿will surely bring you back to a return﴾, transmitted that he said: it is Paradise, and he named it *ma'ad* either because the Prophet ﷺ entered it during the Night Journey and Ascension (*al-Isra' wa al-Mi'raj*, the Prophet's night journey and ascent to heaven) and other occasions, or because Adam, peace be upon him, was in it, so it is a return for his offspring.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He only said this because the word *al-ma'ad* indicates that the one addressed had been in a state to which he would return. Although this appears in the wording, it is appropriate to call something a *ma'ad* as long as the person is not in it as a passing stage; and because these are states that follow the *ma'ad*, which is the rising from the graves.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾, etc. Some of the exegetes said: this is the beginning of a statement whose content is an enumeration of the blessing upon Muhammad ﷺ, and that Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, showed him a mercy which he had not reckoned and which his hope had not reached. Others said: rather, His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And you did not expect﴾ etc. is a statement linked to His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained for you the Qur'an﴾, meaning: while you were in the condition of one who does not expect that. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿is bestowed upon you﴾ is an expression for the declaration of prophethood and the conveyance of the Qur'an, as you say: "So-and-so conveyed to so-and-so the leadership," and the like. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ is in the accusative as a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*). *Al-zahir* (supporter) means the helper. The meaning is: strive, O Muhammad, in your conveyance, and do not soften, and do not falter, so that his support for the disbelievers would be in this manner, that is, by slackening toward them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 28, verse 87–88:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And let them not turn you away from the signs of Allah after they have been sent down to you. Call to your Lord, and do not be among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿And do not invoke another god alongside Allah. There is no god but Him. Everything will perish except His Face. To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: "And let them not turn you away" means: by their words, their lies, and their harm. Do not pay attention to them, and proceed with your affair. Ya'qub read "wa la yasuddanka" with the nun jussed (wa la yasuddankə, with the final nun vowelless). His saying: "Call to your Lord" and the whole verse contains conciliation (al-muhadana) and peaceful coexistence (al-muwada'a), and all of this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword.

The occasion of this verse was that the Quraysh would invite the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to venerate their idols, and at that point Satan cast into his recitation the matter of the cranes (amr al-gharaniq).

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾ is a prohibition against what they were upon, so they are the intended meaning even though the wording is free of mention of them. His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿except His Face﴾: one group said it is an expression for the Essence (al-dhat), and the meaning is: perishing except Him. This was said by al-Tabari and a group including Abu al-Ma'ali, may Allah have mercy on him. Al-Zajjaj said: except Him (illa iyyahu). Sufyan al-Thawri said: the intended meaning is: except what is performed for His Face, that is, what is done for His sake of obedience and turning toward Him by it. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ .......... The Lord of the servants, toward Him is the face and the deed

And from it is the saying of the speaker: "I intended by my action the Face of Allah, the Exalted." And from it is the saying of His, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face﴾ [al-An'am: 52].

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ means the decisive ruling and its execution in this world and the Hereafter. His saying: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ is an announcement of the gathering (al-hashr) and the return from the graves. The majority read "turja'un" with the ta' and a fatha on the jim. 'Isa read "yarji'un" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim, and Abu 'Amr read both ways.

The tafsir of Surat al-Qasas is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

And blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: the intended meaning is: except what is performed for His Face, that is, what is done for His sake of obedience and turning toward Him by it. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ .......... The Lord of the servants, toward Him is the face and the deed

And from it is the saying of the speaker: "I intended by my action the Face of Allah, the Exalted." And from it is the saying of His, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face﴾ [al-An'am: 52].

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ means the decisive ruling and its execution in this world and the Hereafter. His saying: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ is an announcement of the gathering (al-hashr) and the return from the graves. The majority read "turja'un" with the ta' and a fatha on the jim. 'Isa read "yarji'un" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim, and Abu 'Amr read both ways.

The tafsir of Surat al-Qasas is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

And blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.
